one_liner: Schema-first binary serializer with C#, TypeScript, Rust and C++ codegen; its C# decoder beat Google.Protobuf and MessagePack 4-9x.
what_it_does: Bebop is a schema language and compiler (bebopc) that generates typed encode/decode code for C#, TypeScript, Rust, C, C++, Dart and Python from .bop files. You declare structs (fixed field lists that can never change), messages (indexed, optional fields that can evolve) and unions, then call the generated methods, e.g. BebopSerializer.Encode(record), Decode<T>(bytes) or record.EncodeIntoBuffer(byte[]) in C#. It does not replace Protobuf in place: the IDL and wire format are different (Protobuf-format support is an open request, #73), and its RPC layer is its own (Tempo), not gRPC.
how_it_is_fast: The wire format uses fixed-width little-endian integers and IEEE floats. There are no varints and no per-field wire-type tags, so the C# runtime reads each value with one unaligned load (Unsafe.ReadUnaligned over a ReadOnlySpan<byte>) and writes it with WriteUnaligned. bebopc emits straight-line code for each type: a struct is a fixed sequence of reads with no tags or length prefix, and a message is a uint32 body length plus 1-byte field indices handled by a switch loop. The native guid type (16 raw bytes) and date type (8-byte tick count) need no string or sub-message conversion, and float arrays are block-copied through MemoryMarshal.AsBytes. It is not zero-copy: decode copies strings and byte arrays into managed objects.
when_to_use: .NET 8+ services that decode many small or medium records where decode latency dominates. In the cited run, a two-int32 record decoded in 11.9 ns against 85.5 ns for Google.Protobuf.
Systems where several languages share one schema (C#, TypeScript, Rust, C/C++, Dart, Python), e.g. a browser client talking to a .NET server.
Record shapes that will never change, which you can declare as a struct. Structs are the fastest and most compact Bebop encoding (166 ns vs 232 ns for the message form on the complex decode).
Hot send paths that can reuse buffers: EncodeIntoBuffer(byte[]) sized by MaxByteCount and backed by ArrayPool avoids the allocation of the default Encode().
Payloads with many GUIDs, timestamps or float arrays. Bebop stores these natively instead of as strings or sub-messages.
when_not_to_use: You need Protobuf wire compatibility or the gRPC ecosystem. Bebop's format is its own.

Wire size matters for small integers. With fixed-width ints and no varints, a two-int32 record is 8 B (struct) or 15 B (message), against 6 B for Protobuf and 7 B for MessagePack; the simple record is 48-57 B against 42 B.

Allocation-sensitive code that serializes through the default Encode(). It starts from an empty buffer, doubles it as it grows, then copies with ToArray. The complex struct allocated 1,032 B, against 400 B for Protobuf and 304 B for MessagePack.
Big-endian hosts: the C# BebopReader and BebopWriter throw on them. Also .NET Framework or runtimes before .NET 8 on current 3.x packages.

Untrusted input, or reading one field of a large message. Decoders trust the uint32 length prefixes (generated C# allocates an array of the declared length before reading its elements), and no hardening guidance is documented. The maintainer also says Bebop is record-oriented, so it has no FlatBuffers-style partial reads.

integration.form: module: NuGet package `bebop` (C# runtime) plus the bebopc code generator (bebop-tools on NuGet, npm or cargo). The C++ runtime is a single header, Runtime/C++/src/bebop.hpp.
integration.dependencies: none at runtime (the bebop 3.2.3 nuspec lists no dependencies); code generation needs the bebopc binary
integration.min_toolchain: .NET 8: bebop 3.2.3 targets net8.0 and net9.0 and uses static abstract interface members. The C# getting-started page still lists .NET Framework 4.7.2 and .NET Core 3.1, which is out of date. Generated C++ needs C++17 (std::optional, std::variant); the runtime test builds with g++ -std=c++17.
integration.platforms: Little-endian only in C#. bebopc ships prebuilt for Linux, macOS and Windows on x64 and arm64, plus a WASI .wasm build.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. In the source, each C# encode/decode call creates its own ref-struct BebopReader/BebopWriter with no shared mutable state. The TypeScript runtime reuses one process-wide BebopView.

gotchas: The C# BebopWriter.WriteDate converts a DateTime to whole milliseconds since the Unix epoch before writing 100 ns ticks. Sub-millisecond precision is lost on round-trip, and all dates come back as UTC.

Messages encode fields in declaration order. When an old reader hits an unknown field index, the generated decoder jumps to the end of the message, so it drops any known fields encoded after the new one. Field indices are also a single byte.
Structs cannot evolve. Adding or removing a field breaks every existing reader, per the docs.
TypeScript: encode() returns a subarray of a shared singleton BebopView, so the next encode overwrites earlier results unless you copy them (issue #209, open since 2022).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Bebop over HyperSerializer when data crosses language boundaries or needs schema evolution. HyperSerializer is .NET-only and serializes types positionally with no contract, while Bebop generates code for six-plus languages from one .bop schema with versionable messages. Pick SBE instead for fixed-layout, low-latency financial messaging; its code generator runs as a Java jar, while bebopc is a native binary.
verified_claims_summary: The run is ProgrammerAL/SerializationBenchmarks (BenchmarkDotNet 0.13.1 in Release, .NET 5.0.9 x64 RyuJIT, Ryzen 9 3950X, Windows, 2021). Bebop 2.2.6 decoded a complex record in 166 ns (struct) and 232 ns (message), against 1,051 ns for Google.Protobuf 3.17.3 and 1,585 ns for MessagePack-CSharp 2.3.75, and decoded a like-for-like two-int32 record in 11.9 ns against 85.5 ns for Protobuf. Serialize gains were smaller (1.07-3.9x over Protobuf). The complex schemas differ (Protobuf uses a string GUID and Timestamp sub-messages), which widens the complex-decode gap.
status_note: Active: last push 2026-02-17, latest release v3.2.3 on 2025-09-16, Apache-2.0, and the runtime has no dependencies. But the only independent numbers are from 2021 (Bebop 2.2.6 on .NET 5), and the docs lag the code: the supported .NET list is stale and the known-issues page reads 'TODO'.
